Yes, sugar is widely recognized as the primary dietary cause of cavities, though the full mechanism involves bacteria as well [d1][d8]. According to the WHO, "free sugars are the essential dietary factor in the development of dental caries," as bacteria in the mouth metabolize sugars to produce acid that demineralizes tooth enamel and dentine [d1]. Nationwide Children's Hospital similarly states that "cavities are caused by sugar and a type of bacteria living in the mouth," with bacteria converting sugar into acid that eats into enamel [d8]. Healthline and other sources confirm that harmful bacteria feed on dietary sugar and produce acids that weaken and destroy enamel, forming cavities [d4][d7]. Some sources add nuance: carbohydrates more broadly (bread, rice, potatoes) also break down into sugars that fuel bacterial acid production, and poor oral hygiene compounds the risk [d9][d3][d2]. Nonetheless, the consistent consensus across sources is that sugar is the primary dietary driver of tooth decay [d6][d1].
